findings.title: No rule for WHEN validation fires (blur vs change vs submit)
findings.principle: Every form field validates on blur (first pass) and on every keystroke thereafter only if that field is already in an error state (re-validate to clear it fast); no field may show a validation error while the user is still typing into it for the first time, and no field may wait past blur to reveal an error it already knows about at submit time. The submit button performs a final full-form validation pass but is not the first time an error may appear.
findings.why: Without a stated firing rule, every new form re-derives its own timing from scratch, and the codebase already shows the two opposite failure modes coexisting: forms that validate only on submit (so a user discovers a mistake made three fields ago only after finishing the whole form) and, if a future contributor free-hands 'live' validation, forms that flash an error before the user has finished typing (the exact anti-pattern Baymard/NN/g flag). Neither is written down as banned or required anywhere in the estate.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/auth/register/page.tsx:88-115 (StepRegister.handleSubmit): min-age, password-length, and password-strength checks all run only inside handleSubmit, gated behind e.preventDefault(), with zero per-field onBlur handler anywhere in the file (grep for onBlur in this file returns nothing). The user can fill email, password, and birthday, click submit, and only then learn the password was too short. Contrast with the field-level FieldHelper primitive (_design-system/COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md line 64) which exists specifically to render inline under-field errors but is never imported by this form (0 external call-sites verified in the registry's own audit note).
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn -i 'on blur|onblur|on submit|onsubmit|on change|onchange|debounce|as.you.type|as-you-type|real.time valid|live valid|premature' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md -> zero hits for validation-timing language (onChange/onSubmit hits that exist are unrelated event-handler-detection code, not a validation-timing rule). grep -rn -i 'validation should not fire prematurely' _design-system _rules _docs CLAUDE.md -> zero hits; the only place this exact NN/g principle appears is _design-system/research/TASTE_CHECKOUT.md:16, scoped explicitly to the payment/checkout screen research file, never generalized.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _design-system/research/TASTE_CHECKOUT.md item 10 states 'validation should not fire prematurely mid-typing' but only as a checkout-flow research finding (T1/T2 sourced), never promoted into LOCKFILE or SOURCE as a project-wide form rule, and never given a firing-timing rule at all (blur-then-live-clear is not stated anywhere, checkout doc or otherwise). Delta: the WHEN (blur, then live-clear) and the ON-SUBMIT-ONLY anti-pattern currently shipping in auth/register are both undocumented.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md, new subsection under §14 (next to §14.4 Flow escape hatches, which already owns error-copy rules) titled 'Validation timing'
findings.enforcement: checklist item in the design-verifier's per-screen scorecard for any form; a gate is hard here (requires interaction simulation, not static grep) so start with a manual scorecard row, not a static hook

findings.title: Field-level errors ship as toasts, violating the estate's own locked error-placement rule, with nothing enforcing the split
findings.principle: A validation error caused by ONE field's value (format, length, range, a business-rule check on that field) renders as an inline FieldHelper under that exact field; toast.error() is reserved for whole-form or server/network failures that are not attributable to a single visible field. A code review or gate must reject a diff that adds toast.error(...) inside a handler whose preceding lines are single-field checks (password.length, age-from-birthdate, format regex).
findings.why: The estate already legislated this split (LOCKFILE §14.4: 'Field errors sit UNDER the field... banner errors only for whole-form failures') but wrote no mechanism that catches a violation, so the rule already has at least one live breach in production code. A rule with zero enforcement and a demonstrated breach is the exact 'compliant but unfinished' failure mode named in this project's own FLOORS LAW preamble, just applied to forms instead of visual density.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/auth/register/page.tsx:89 toast.error(t('errorMinAge')) and line 96 toast.error(t('errorPasswordMin')) and line 100 toast.error(tp(...)) are all single-field checks (birthday field, password field) rendered as toasts, not as FieldHelper under the birthday/password inputs, directly contradicting LOCKFILE.md:1363-1366's own text pasted two lines above in the same rule ('The email addresses don't match.'/'Password needs at least 8 characters.' examples are field-specific, yet the shipped code toasts them).
findings.existing_coverage: yes, but unenforced: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md:1358-1366 (§14.4) states the exact split and even the exact password-length wording used as its own example. The delta is purely enforcement: no gate, lint rule, or registry note flags toast.error() called inside a single-field validation branch.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new PreToolUse or CI-time hook alongside the existing drift gates (.claude/hooks/), e.g. field-error-toast-gate; cross-reference from LOCKFILE §14.4 itself so the rule text names its own enforcement
findings.enforcement: gate: field-error-toast-gate (static heuristic: flag toast.error/toast.warning calls inside a form's onSubmit whose immediate preceding condition tests a single named form-state variable rather than a response/catch block)

findings.title: Autofill and password-manager compatibility (autoComplete/inputMode/aria-invalid) is undocumented and missing from exactly the two forms it matters most for
findings.principle: Every input that maps to a known browser/password-manager autofill category (email, current-password, new-password, name, tel, birthdate, address fields, one-time-code) carries the matching HTML autocomplete token per the WHATWG autofill spec, and every input whose keyboard should differ from the default text keyboard carries the matching inputMode. This applies to auth/login and auth/register before any other form in the app, because credential save/fill is the single highest-value autofill moment in the product.
findings.why: Without explicit autocomplete tokens, iOS/Android/desktop password managers cannot reliably classify a field, so a returning user's saved Solen credentials may not offer to autofill on login, and a new user's password may not get offered a save/generate prompt on signup, both of which raise drop-off on the two forms every single account holder must pass through. This is also a literal accessibility success criterion, not just a nicety.
findings.local_evidence: grep across app/ finds only 3 files with real (non-showcase) autoComplete usage: app/[locale]/booking/lookup/page.tsx, app/[locale]/booking/resend-link/page.tsx, and app/[locale]/profile/settings/SettingsForm.tsx. The two forms where this matters most have zero: components-legacy/auth/SignIn.tsx (the live component rendered at /auth/login, both the email/password form at lines 205-221 and the password-reset form at line 176) has no autoComplete attribute on any of its 3 inputs; app/[locale]/auth/register/page.tsx has no autoComplete on its email (line 156), password (line 164), salon-name (line 198), or birthday-date (line 212) inputs. Total repo count: 137 raw <input> elements in app/, only 17 inputMode usages, only 8 aria-invalid usages (concentrated in TextInput.tsx/Select.tsx/Textarea.tsx primitives plus 2 standalone pages), only 24 autoComplete usages including the primitive's own doc-comment and the dev showcase page.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'autocomplete|autofill|password manager|inputmode' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md _design-system/COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md _rules/*.md CLAUDE.md -> zero hits anywhere in the law estate; the concept does not exist as a written rule at any tier.
findings.existing_coverage: none. TextInput.tsx (the primitive) forwards ...inputProps so autoComplete/inputMode CAN be passed through, but nothing requires callers to pass them, and the two highest-stakes forms (login, register) do not even use the TextInput primitive, they hand-roll raw <input> tags.
findings.outside_reference: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) requires programmatically-determined autocomplete values on inputs collecting user identity/contact data; WHATWG HTML autofill field spec defines the current-password/new-password/email/tel tokens directly relevant here.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md new row in the design contract table (or a new §3.6 next to the existing input-focus §), plus a COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md note on TextInput requiring autoComplete/inputMode as a documented prop convention
findings.enforcement: gate: autofill-attr-gate (static grep on new/edited <input type="email"|"password"|"tel"> literals lacking a sibling autoComplete= on the same JSX element)

findings.title: Multi-step form state is memory-only and lost on refresh/back-nav across at least two flows, with no project-wide recovery law
findings.principle: Any multi-step form or wizard that takes a user more than 2 steps to complete must survive an accidental hard refresh or tab close without losing entered data: either persist step state to sessionStorage/localStorage keyed per-flow, write completed steps to the server incrementally (as the dashboard setup wizard already does), or, at minimum, warn the user via beforeunload when they have unsaved multi-step progress and would otherwise lose it silently.
findings.why: A wizard that resets to step 1 on refresh with zero warning converts an accidental tab-close or pull-to-refresh into total data loss for the user, with no way to know it happened until they notice they are back at the start. This is a known, named risk in the booking flow already, and the same architecture (in-memory-only React state, no persistence) repeats in the customer onboarding flow, so the risk is systemic, not a one-off.
findings.local_evidence: _docs/FRONTEND.md:438 and :451 state directly: 'Single in-memory useReducer context (lib/booking-context.tsx) is the whole state carrier; no localStorage/URL persistence of in-progress state, a hard refresh resets the flow' and '⚠️ In-memory-only state: no persistence means an accidental refresh or deep back-nav past step 1 loses the whole cart... a real drop-off risk with no recovery.' The same pattern repeats independently in app/[locale]/onboarding/OnboardingFlow.tsx:66-71 (plain useState for step index and answers, no storage write) — grep for localStorage/sessionStorage in that file returns only a dead referral-code write unrelated to onboarding progress. By contrast app/[locale]/dashboard/setup/page.tsx DOES persist per-step via server fetch (line 34, 48), proving the safer pattern already exists in the codebase but was not carried to the two customer-facing flows.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'hard refresh|persist.*step|wizard.*persist|localStorage|sessionStorage' _design-system/*.md _docs/*.md -> the only hits are the FRONTEND.md lines quoted above, which describe the CURRENT gap as an incompleteness note inside a flow-map document, not as a LAW instructing future flows to avoid it. No hit in LOCKFILE.md, SOURCE.md, or COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: FRONTEND.md documents the exact defect as 'acceptable per design' for the booking wizard specifically (resetForm-on-success is called out as deliberate), but that acceptance is scoped to booking's post-success reset, not to the refresh-mid-flow data-loss case, and nothing generalizes the finding into a rule new multi-step surfaces must follow.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md §14 (Flow escape hatches is the closest existing home) or a new component doc for a shared usePersistedWizardState hook
findings.enforcement: checklist item in the design-verifier scorecard for any new multi-step surface; longer-term a shared hook (usePersistedWizardState) that new wizards are required to use per COMPONENT_REGISTRY convention

findings.title: Double-submit protection uses a real mutex (ref) in exactly one flow; everywhere else it is React-state-only, which has a known race
findings.principle: Any control that triggers a non-idempotent write (create booking, create payment intent, submit a review, send a refund request) must guard against a double-fire with a synchronous ref/lock checked BEFORE the async call starts, not only a React state flag used to disable the button, because state-only disabling can still race a fast double-click/double-tap ahead of the re-render that disables the control. The guard pattern already shipped in the booking payment flow (a boolean useRef checked and set before the network call, not after) is the reference implementation for every other single-fire mutation in the app.
findings.why: A state-only 'disabled={loading}' guard depends on React re-rendering the DOM before the second click lands; on a slow device or a fast double-tap this is not guaranteed, and for a money-moving or write-once action a duplicate submission can create two bookings, two payment intents, or two reviews from one user action. The codebase itself already discovered and fixed this exact race for booking payments but did not turn the fix into a shared, named pattern other mutating forms are required to copy.
findings.local_evidence: components-legacy/booking/PayConfirmStep.tsx:111-112 and :217 explicitly comment 'chargeRef guards against a double-create from a re-render / double-tap while the create round-trip is in flight,' i.e. a ref-based mutex distinct from and in addition to the isSubmitting state flag at line 64. Grep for the same ref-guard idiom (useRef.*guard|inFlightRef|submitRef|chargeRef) across app/ and components-legacy/ returns only 7 files total, and only PayConfirmStep.tsx uses it for a financial mutation; other write-triggering forms (SettingsForm.tsx save/delete handlers, register/page.tsx signup, dashboard ConfirmModal delete actions) rely solely on a state boolean (setSaving(true)/disabled={saving}).
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'double.submit|double submit|debounce.*submit|prevent.*duplicate|idempot' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md -> zero hits; idempotency language exists only in _rules/LESSONS_LEARNED.md and two Stripe dispute-refund API routes (app/api/bookings/[id]/report/route.ts, app/api/admin/booking-disputes/[id]/action/route.ts), i.e. server-side idempotency keys for a narrow admin/dispute path, never a UI-layer double-submit rule.
findings.existing_coverage: none as a UI-layer rule; the closest relative is server-side Stripe idempotency_key usage in two admin routes, which solves the same class of problem but on the backend only and is not cross-referenced from any frontend forms doc.
findings.outside_reference: Stripe's own integration guidance requires client-side double-submit prevention in addition to server idempotency keys, precisely because network latency plus a fast double-click can fire two requests before either resolves.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md or a new lib/hooks/useSubmitGuard.ts pattern documented in COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md, referenced from any Button/form doc for a 'commit' action
findings.enforcement: gate: hard to write generically as static analysis; start as a documented required hook (useSubmitGuard) and a code-review checklist line for any new POST-triggering handler on a financial or write-once action

findings.title: Destructive-action confirmation has three competing mechanisms in production with no rule choosing between them
findings.principle: A destructive action (delete, cancel, refund, remove) that cannot be undone within the same view must use the shared Modal primitive with an explicit two-button confirm/cancel footer stating the specific consequence ('Delete this review? This cannot be undone.'), never the browser-native window.confirm(). A destructive action that CAN be trivially undone in place (e.g. removing one chip from a multi-select before submitting) does not need a blocking dialog at all. Every dashboard page implementing its own local confirm modal must migrate to the shared Modal primitive rather than hand-rolling a new one.
findings.why: window.confirm() cannot be styled, blocks the JS thread, cannot carry the design system's type/spacing/color rules, and reads as a raw browser dialog with the page's URL in the title bar, a visibly different product experience from every other Solen surface. Meanwhile 8 separate dashboard pages hand-roll their own bespoke confirm modal instead of the one shared Modal primitive, meaning even the non-native path is inconsistent screen to screen, so a delete confirmation may look and behave differently depending on which dashboard page the salon owner happens to be on.
findings.local_evidence: grep confirms 3 live window.confirm() call sites remain (app/[locale]/dashboard/reviews/page.tsx:137 window.confirm(t('deleteReplyConfirm'))), alongside two code comments in app/[locale]/queue/[token]/page.tsx (lines 141, 580) noting the team already replaced window.confirm() with the Modal primitive for that ONE flow specifically, implying the team knows window.confirm() is the wrong pattern but has not swept it project-wide. COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md:51 itself documents, in its own audit note, that 8 dashboard pages (all-salons, all-users, staff, services, badge-manager, bookings, review-moderation, calendar) each hand-roll a local ConfirmModal/StaffModal/ServiceModal/etc. instead of using the shared Modal.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'destructive|are you sure|window.confirm|confirm.*delete' _design-system/*.md -> the only hits are a CONSISTENCY_AUDIT.md line noting 'a few destructive-red fills' as a logged-but-deferred minor skip, and no rule anywhere bans window.confirm() or mandates the shared Modal for destructive actions specifically.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md documents the Modal primitive and separately documents the 8-page consolidation debt as a known fact, but treats it purely as a component-reuse/consolidation problem, not as a live UX inconsistency in how destructive actions are confirmed, and never states the window.confirm()-is-banned rule explicitly.
findings.outside_reference: Nielsen Norman Group's error-prevention heuristic (heuristic #5 of the 10 usability heuristics) calls for confirmation before high-cost, hard-to-reverse actions, delivered through the product's own UI, not a raw browser primitive.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md new row in the design contract table ('destructive action') plus a Modal.md usage note explicitly banning window.confirm()
findings.enforcement: gate: no-window-confirm-gate (static grep blocking new window.confirm(/confirm( calls in app/**, components-legacy/**)

findings.title: Undo-vs-confirm policy exists only as a single rejected case, not as a general rule
findings.principle: State, as a general policy, which class of action gets a blocking confirm dialog (irreversible, financial, or affects another party: refunds, cancellations that trigger a notification to the other side) versus a toast-with-undo window (reversible, single-party, low-cost: unfavoriting, removing a draft line item, dismissing a notification). Absent this split, every future feature re-litigates it from scratch, and the one data point on record is a rejection of a SPECIFIC undo treatment on a SPECIFIC screen, not a decision against undo-as-a-pattern everywhere.
findings.why: REMOVED.md records the owner rejecting one exact undo implementation (booking-request approve/decline morphing to a committed pill with an undo window) with the verbatim reason 'The p three, no. P three, I don't want that,' which is a rejection of that specific morph/collapse motion treatment on that specific dashboard screen, not a stated rejection of undo-as-a-pattern in general. Nothing in the estate distinguishes this from, say, an undo-toast on a customer favoriting/unfavoriting a salon, which is a completely different risk profile (free, single-party, instantly reversible) from a salon owner declining a paying customer's booking request.
findings.local_evidence: _design-system/REMOVED.md line 74 and _design-system/TASTE_LOG.md line 218 both record only the one P3 rejection; no other undo-pattern decision exists anywhere in either file. grep for 'undo' across all of _design-system/*.md returns only these two lines plus unrelated hits (git undo commentary, spacing-token undo).
findings.absence_proof: grep -ri 'undo' _design-system LOCKFILE.md SOURCE.md TASTE_LOG.md REMOVED.md CLAUDE.md -> total 2 substantive hits, both the same P3 rejection restated in two files; zero hits for a general undo-vs-confirm policy statement.
findings.existing_coverage: none as a general rule; the single existing data point is scoped to one rejected screen and must not be read as a blanket ban on undo patterns, which would itself be a misapplication of the graveyard.
findings.outside_reference: Gmail's undo-send and most modern SaaS toast-undo patterns (Linear, Superhuman) reserve blocking confirms for the smaller set of truly high-cost/irreversible/other-party-affecting actions and use undo-toast for everything else, precisely to avoid the confirm-dialog fatigue Nielsen Norman warns dilutes the effectiveness of confirmation dialogs when overused.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md new subsection near the destructive-action row (states-forms-06), explicitly citing and scoping the P3 REMOVED.md entry so it is not misread as a blanket undo ban
findings.enforcement: checklist / doc-only for now; not mechanically gateable

findings.title: Session-expiry mid-form is an explicitly unbuilt TBD with no user-facing recovery behavior
findings.principle: Any client-side form submission that fails specifically because the session expired (a 401 from the API, distinct from a validation 4xx or a network failure) must show a message naming that cause ('Deine Sitzung ist abgelaufen, bitte melde dich erneut an') and, wherever technically possible, preserve the user's already-entered form values through a re-login round trip (via a return-path redirect that restores the draft), rather than surfacing the same generic save-failed toast as every other error.
findings.why: A user who has been filling a settings form or a long dashboard form for several minutes and whose session silently expires mid-fill currently gets the exact same undifferentiated error toast as a validation failure or a flaky network blip, with no indication that re-authentication (not a retry) is what will fix it, and with their typed content at risk of being lost the moment they navigate to log back in.
findings.local_evidence: _design-system/SOURCE.md:1203 states directly: 'Client components use a useSession hook (TBD, currently checks done in server components only)', i.e. the design system's own source-of-truth document flags client-side session-awareness as not yet built. app/[locale]/profile/settings/SettingsForm.tsx's save/delete/avatar-upload catch blocks (lines 109-116, 141-149, 228-236) all funnel into a generic console.error plus (per the file's toast calls found elsewhere in the same handlers) a generic saveError/actionError toast, with no branch checking res.status === 401 specifically.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'session expir|re-auth|reauth|token refresh' _design-system/*.md _rules/*.md CLAUDE.md -> zero hits for a client-facing session-expiry UX rule; the only 'session' hits found are backend auth-security rules (getSession() vs getUser() JWT verification, _rules/SECURITY_RULES.md), an entirely different concern (server-side identity trust, not the user-facing recovery experience).
findings.existing_coverage: none for the client UX; server-side session verification itself is thoroughly covered and locked (getUser()-only rule, gate-enforced), but that is a security correctness rule, not a forms/UX rule about what the user sees or keeps when their session lapses mid-form.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/SOURCE.md §19.4 (Auth-required pages), extending the existing TBD note into an actual rule once the client useSession hook ships
findings.enforcement: checklist item; blocked on the useSession hook itself being built (a backend/frontend engineering item, not just a docs gap)

findings.title: Error message shapes are inconsistent and frequently fully generic, contradicting the estate's own anti-pattern list
findings.principle: No user-facing error string may consist only of a category label with no cause and no next step ('Aktion fehlgeschlagen', 'Netzwerkfehler', 'Fehler beim Speichern' with no elaboration). Every error string names what failed (which action), and either why (if known and safe to show) or what to do next (retry, check connection, contact support), matching the standard already set by SOURCE.md's own anti-pattern list which explicitly bans a generic 'Network error' toast for everything.
findings.why: A generic error label gives the user no actionable next step and no way to tell a permanent failure (e.g. their card was declined) from a transient one (network blip, worth retrying), which is precisely the distinction SOURCE.md's own anti-pattern section already says must be made ('distinguish RLS / 4xx / 5xx / network'), yet the shipped translation strings do not make it.
findings.local_evidence: messages/de.json contains, among others: line 533 'networkError': 'Netzwerkfehler' (bare category label, no next step), line 1332/1367 'actionError': 'Aktion fehlgeschlagen' (no cause, no next step, reused identically at two different call sites for two different actions), line 1809/1824 'saveError': 'Fehler beim Speichern.' (no cause, no next step). Counting distinct error-message translation keys referenced across just the toast.error() call sites sampled in app/ turned up at least 15 differently-named keys (saveError, actionError, rejectError, approveError, cancelFailed, networkError, removeFailed, errorProcessing, errorResetPassword, confirmFailed, among others), each independently worded rather than composed from a shared 'what failed + why + next step' template.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'generic.*error|error.*generic' _design-system/*.md -> exactly one hit, SOURCE.md:1208 '❌ Generic "Network error" toast for everything, distinguish RLS / 4xx / 5xx / network', which states the anti-pattern but gives no positive template for what a compliant message must contain, and is not cross-referenced from the field-error rule in LOCKFILE §14.4 (states-forms-02), so the two related rules live in different documents with no link between them.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the anti-pattern is named once (SOURCE.md:1208) but with no positive spec of message content (what/why/next), no connection to the separately-locked LOCKFILE §14.4 field-error-content rule, and evidently no enforcement, since the shipped translation strings violate it today.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/SOURCE.md §19 (Error handling), turning the existing anti-pattern bullet into a positive content template, cross-linked to LOCKFILE §14.4
findings.enforcement: checklist / manual review of new translation keys; a lint rule flagging error-* i18n keys under N characters (a bare-label proxy) is a plausible cheap gate

findings.title: Read-only field state is entirely absent from the component and code layer
findings.principle: Add a read-only visual state to the shared TextInput/Select/Textarea primitives, visually distinct from both the editable-at-rest state and the disabled state (read-only = the value is final and viewable but not because the control is unavailable, e.g. a confirmed email on a settings page, a locked booking reference), and require any field that is 'this value cannot change here' (as opposed to 'this control is temporarily unusable') to use it instead of the disabled state.
findings.why: Disabled and read-only communicate different things to a user (disabled implies 'not right now, maybe later'; read-only implies 'this is fixed, by design') and to a screen reader (a disabled input is removed from the tab order and announced as unavailable; a read-only input remains focusable and selectable, e.g. so its value can be copied), so collapsing both into the single existing 'disabled' state loses real information for both sighted and assistive-tech users.
findings.local_evidence: grep for readOnly across the entire app/ tree returns zero results (no code usage anywhere), and TextInput.tsx/Select.tsx/Textarea.tsx's documented prop surface (tone?: default|error|warning|success[|active], loading?, revealable?) in COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md lines 58-63 lists no read-only tone or prop at all.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n -i 'readonly|read-only|read only' _design-system/COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md -> the only 3 hits are unrelated (archived-files-are-read-only-history, a doc-reference-is-read-only note, a subagent-tool-is-read-only note); the word never appears in the context of an input/field component state.
findings.existing_coverage: none. The full state matrix implied by the design system (default, hover, focus, active, selected, disabled, loading, error, empty, success) as enumerated across COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md and LOCKFILE.md never lists read-only as a member of that matrix.
findings.outside_reference: WAI-ARIA / WCAG treat aria-readonly and the disabled state as distinct semantics precisely because they have different keyboard/focus/announcement behavior; this is a standards-level distinction, not a stylistic preference.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/components/TextInput.md (new) or a TextInput.tsx prop addition, registered in COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md
findings.enforcement: doc-only / component API addition; not gateable until the prop exists
